title: PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation
hook: Full agentic evals like SWE-Bench and GAIA can cost thousands of dollars and days to run — PACE predicts those scores from a tiny, cheap subset of ordinary benchmarks, at under 1% of the cost.
key_points: Agentic benchmarks (SWE-Bench, GAIA) are accurate but expensive — a single full evaluation can cost thousands of dollars and take days.
PACE builds a proxy benchmark by selecting non-agentic evaluation instances whose scores best predict performance on a target agentic benchmark, via regression.
Instance selection blends two strategies: target-relevance (locally similar instances) and global informativeness.

Across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks: leave-one-out MAE under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, ~85% pairwise model-ranking accuracy — all under 1% of full agentic-eval cost.
Also reveals which atomic skills each agentic benchmark actually demands, since the proxy instances selected differ by benchmark.
content_html: Evaluating an LLM agent on SWE-Bench or GAIA is the gold standard for measuring agentic capability, but it's slow and expensive — a single run can cost thousands of dollars and take days. Non-agentic benchmarks testing individual capabilities are cheap and fast by comparison. PACE asks whether the cheap ones can stand in for the expensive ones.
extra_html:
Predicting an expensive score from a cheap subset

PACE constructs a proxy benchmark by picking instances from existing non-agentic evaluations whose aggregate scores most reliably predict a model's performance on a target agentic benchmark, fitting a regression from the compact subset's scores to the full agentic score. The instance pool is curated by combining two complementary strategies: selecting instances locally relevant to the target benchmark, and selecting instances that are globally informative across many models. Applying this to four target agentic benchmarks yields PACE-Bench, the concrete proxy the authors evaluate.

Why it matters

Across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic source benchmarks, PACE-Bench predicts agentic scores with leave-one-out mean absolute error under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and roughly 85% pairwise model-ranking accuracy — all for well under 1% of the cost of running the full agentic evaluation. Beyond the cost savings, examining which proxy instances get selected for each benchmark reveals which underlying atomic skills that benchmark is actually testing, which is useful for anyone trying to understand what a headline agentic score is really measuring.
